## Spread spectrum modulation

- **Problem statement:** How can a narrowband signal ($m[n]$) be transmitted in the presence of interference?

    - if an intereference occupies the same frequency, $m[n]$ may be completely masked by the interference, and it cannot be detected or demodulated.


::: {.fragment}
::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
- **Solution:** What if we could spread the signal over a much wider bandwidth with a lower power spectral density?

    - Maybe in this case the interference would not be able to (fully) mask the signal, and it could be detected and demodulated.

[[Hedy Kiesler Markey (Lamarr) and George Antheil patented \acr{FHSS} in 1941.](https://patents.google.com/patent/US2292387A/en)]{style="font-size: 0.4em; color: gray;"}

:::

::: {.column}
![](assets/figures/patent__lamarr__secret_comm_system.png){width=50%}
:::

:::
:::



### Spread spectrum modulation principle




[- By multiplying the information-bearing waveform ($m[n]$) by a much faster pseudorandom sequence ($c[n]$), the transmitted energy is spread over a much wider bandwidth, producing a nearly flat power spectral density.]{style="font-size: 60%;"}



```{python}
from IPython.display import HTML
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import plotly.io as pio

# Frequency axis (normalized to the carrier frequency)
f = np.linspace(-5, 5, 2001);

# Narrowband signal: Gaussian-shaped PSD concentrated around DC
sigma_n = 0.35;
psd_narrow = np.exp(-(f / sigma_n) ** 2); # Max value is 1 at f=0

# Calculate area of narrowband signal using numerical integration
area_narrow = np.trapz(psd_narrow, f);

# Spread-spectrum signal: Gaussian-shaped over a wider bandwidth
sigma_c = 2.0; # Wider sigma for spread spectrum
psd_spread_raw = np.exp(-(f / sigma_c) ** 2); # Max value is 1 at f=0

# Calculate area of raw spread-spectrum signal
area_spread_raw = np.trapz(psd_spread_raw, f);

# Scale spread-spectrum signal to have the same area as narrowband signal
scale_factor = area_narrow / area_spread_raw;
psd_spread = scale_factor * psd_spread_raw;

# Interfering signal: Gaussian-shaped, designed to almost mask the narrowband signal
sigma_i = 0.1;
peak_amplitude_i = 1.4;
frequency_shift = 0.2; # Shift the interfering signal to the right
psd_interfering = peak_amplitude_i * np.exp(-((f - frequency_shift) / sigma_i) ** 2);

# Noise floor for visualization
noise_floor = 0.4 * np.ones_like(f);

fig = go.Figure();
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=f, y=psd_narrow, mode='lines', name='Narrowband (s)', line=dict(color='royalblue', width=3)));
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=f, y=psd_interfering, mode='lines', name='Interfering Signal', line=dict(color='red', width=3), visible=True));
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=f, y=psd_spread, mode='lines', name='Spread spectrum (c)', line=dict(color='green', width=3), visible=True));
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=f, y=noise_floor, mode='lines', name='Noise Floor', line=dict(color='gray', width=1, dash='dot'), visible=True));

# Define bandwidths (e.g., 2*sigma as a proxy for effective bandwidth)
B_s = 2 * sigma_n;
B_c = 2 * sigma_c;
B_i = 2 * sigma_i;

# Define y-coordinates for the bandwidth arrows and annotations
# Place narrowband arrow slightly above its peak (which is 1)
arrow_y_narrow = 1.05;
# Place interfering signal arrow at a higher level to avoid overlap
arrow_y_interfering = np.max(psd_interfering) + 0.2;
# Place spread spectrum arrow slightly above its peak (which is scale_factor)
arrow_y_spread = np.max(psd_spread) + 0.05;

fig.update_layout(
    title='Spread Spectrum modulation principle',
    xaxis_title='Frequency',
    yaxis_title='Power Spectral Density',
    template='plotly_white',
    legend=dict(orientation='h', yanchor='bottom', y=1.02, xanchor='right', x=1),
    margin=dict(l=50, r=20, t=50, b=50),
    height=300,
    width=820,
    annotations=[
        # Narrowband bandwidth text label
        dict(
            x=0, y=arrow_y_narrow + 0.05,
            text=f'B<sub>s</sub>',
            showarrow=False,
            font=dict(color="royalblue", size=12),
            yanchor="bottom"
        ),
        # Narrowband bandwidth double-sided arrow
        dict(
            x=B_s/2, y=arrow_y_narrow,
            ax=-B_s/2, ay=arrow_y_narrow,
            xref="x", yref="y", axref="x", ayref="y",
            showarrow=True,
            arrowhead=3, arrowsize=1, arrowwidth=2, arrowcolor="royalblue",
            arrowside="start+end"
        ),
        # Interfering signal bandwidth text label
        dict(
            x=frequency_shift, y=arrow_y_interfering + 0.05,
            text=f'B<sub>i</sub>',
            showarrow=False,
            font=dict(color="red", size=12),
            yanchor="bottom",
            visible=True
        ),
        # Interfering signal bandwidth double-sided arrow
        dict(
            x=frequency_shift + B_i/2, y=arrow_y_interfering,
            ax=frequency_shift - B_i/2, ay=arrow_y_interfering,
            xref="x", yref="y", axref="x", ayref="y",
            showarrow=True,
            arrowhead=3, arrowsize=1, arrowwidth=2, arrowcolor="red",
            arrowside="start+end",
            visible=True
        ),
        # Spread spectrum bandwidth text label
        dict(
            x=0, y=arrow_y_spread + 0.05,
            text=f'B<sub>c</sub>',
            showarrow=False,
            font=dict(color="green", size=12),
            yanchor="bottom",
            visible=True
        ),
        # Spread spectrum bandwidth double-sided arrow
        dict(
            x=B_c/2, y=arrow_y_spread,
            ax=-B_c/2, ay=arrow_y_spread,
            xref="x", yref="y", axref="x", ayref="y",
            showarrow=True,
            arrowhead=3, arrowsize=1, arrowwidth=2, arrowcolor="green",
            arrowside="start+end",
            visible=True
        )
    ]
);

# Remove numerical x-ticks and y-ticks for a qualitative plot
fig.update_xaxes(showticklabels=False);
fig.update_yaxes(showticklabels=False, range=[0, 1.5]); # Keep range for consistent visual scale
HTML(pio.to_html(fig, full_html=False, include_plotlyjs='cdn', include_mathjax=False))
```



[- The signal bandwidth increases dramatically ($B_s \Rightarrow B_c$), but the power density in any given narrow slice of spectrum decreases. Any narrowband interference will only affect a small portion of the spread spectrum signal, and the receiver can still detect and demodulate the signal.]{style="font-size: 60%;"}


### Direct Sequence Spread Spectrum

[\acr{DSSS} is a spread spectrum technique in which the data signal is multiplied by a pseudorandom noise (PN) sequence, also known as a spreading code. The PN sequence has a much higher frequency than the data signal, resulting in a wider bandwidth for the transmitted signal]{style="font-size: 0.8em;"}


$$
\tiny
\color{green}{m(t)} = \color{green}{\sum_{n=-\inf}^{\inf} m_n \cdot \prod\left( \frac{t-n\cdot T_{b}}{T_{b}} \right)} \quad;\quad
\color{blue} {c(t)} = \color{magenta}{\sum_{n=-\inf}^{\inf} p[mod(n, N_{chip})] \cdot \prod\left( \frac{t-n\cdot T_{chip}}{T_{chip}} \right)}
$$

[where $T_{b}$ is the message bit duration, $p[n]$ is the \acr{PRN} sequence of length $N_{chip}$, and $T_{chip}$ is the chip duration.]{style="font-size: 0.6em;"}

### Direct Sequence Spread Spectrum (cont'd)


![](assets/figures/spread_spectrum.svg)

### DSSS signal as train of pulses

- The spreading signal $c(t)$ is a sequence of square pulses (chips) that takes values of +1 or -1 according to the $p[n]$ sequence.

![](assets/figures/spreading_code.svg)

$$
\tiny
\begin{aligned}
c(t) &= \sum_{n=0}^{N_{chips}-1} p[n] \cdot \prod\left( \frac{t-n\cdot T_{chip}}{T_{chip}} \right) \\
     &= \prod\left( \frac{t}{T_{chip}} \right) \ast \sum_{n=0}^{N_{chips}-1} p[n] \cdot \delta(t-n\cdot T_{chip})
\end{aligned}
$$

### Spectrum of DSSS signals

- Can be computed as the product of the square pulse and the train of impulses in the frequency domain

$$
\begin{aligned}
C(f) &= \mathcal{F}\left\lbrace c(t) \right \rbrace \\
     &=  \mathcal{F}\left\lbrace \prod\left( \frac{t}{T_{chip}} \right) \right \rbrace \cdot \sum_{n=0}^{N_{chips}-1} p[n] \cdot e^{-j2\pi f\  n\ T_{chip}} \\
     &= T_{chip} \cdot \text{sinc}(f\ T_{chip}) \cdot \sum_{n=0}^{N_{chips}-1} p[n] \cdot e^{-j2\pi f\  n\ T_{chip}}
\end{aligned}
$$

### Spectrum of DSSS signals (cont'd)

```{python}
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.signal import max_len_seq

# --- Signal Parameters ---
# Chip rate (rate of the PRN code chips)
chip_rate = 1.023e6  # Example: 1.023 MHz for GPS L1 C/A code

# Sampling rate (must be significantly higher than chip_rate)
sampling_rate = 20 * chip_rate  # 10 samples per chip

# Number of chips in one PRN sequence period (e.g., 1023 for GPS C/A code)
num_chips = 1023

# Duration of one chip period
T_chip = 1 / chip_rate

# Duration of the rectangular pulse (assuming it's equal to one chip period)
pulse_width = T_chip

# Total simulation time for one period of the PRN sequence
overall_time = num_chips * T_chip

# Number of samples for the entire signal
num_samples = int(overall_time * sampling_rate)

# Time vector
t = np.linspace(0, overall_time, num_samples, endpoint=False)

prn_chips = 2 * max_len_seq(10)[0][:num_chips] - 1  # Get {-1, 1} and truncate to num_chips if needed

# Upsample the PRN sequence to the sampling rate
samples_per_chip = int(sampling_rate / chip_rate)
prn_sequence = np.repeat(prn_chips, samples_per_chip)

# Ensure the length matches num_samples, trimming or padding if necessary
if len(prn_sequence) > num_samples:
    prn_sequence = prn_sequence[:num_samples]
elif len(prn_sequence) < num_samples:
    # This case should ideally not happen if num_samples is calculated correctly
    prn_sequence = np.pad(prn_sequence, (0, num_samples - len(prn_sequence)), 'edge')
# Create a single rectangular pulse (rect function)
# The pulse will be centered at t=0 for convolution purposes,
# but for direct multiplication, we can create it as a positive-time pulse.

# Number of samples in one pulse width
num_samples_pulse = int(pulse_width * sampling_rate)

# Define a single rectangular pulse (for direct generation/multiplication)
rect_pulse = np.zeros(num_samples)
for i in range(num_chips):
    start_idx = i * samples_per_chip
    end_idx = start_idx + num_samples_pulse
    if end_idx > num_samples:
        end_idx = num_samples # Ensure we don't go out of bounds
    rect_pulse[start_idx:end_idx] = 1.0 # This would be a train of rect pulses


# The PRN sequence defines the amplitude of the individual rect-shaped pulses.
# A simpler and common way to achieve this is to multiply the upsampled PRN sequence
# with a base rectangular pulse train. This is effectively BPSK modulation with rectangular pulses.

# A train of unit rectangular pulses (unmodulated)
unit_pulse_train = np.zeros_like(t)
for i in range(num_chips):
    start_idx = i * samples_per_chip
    end_idx = start_idx + samples_per_chip # Each pulse lasts one chip period
    if start_idx < num_samples:
        unit_pulse_train[start_idx:min(end_idx, num_samples)] = 1.0

# Modulated signal: PRN sequence values applied to the rectangular pulse train
signal_modulated = prn_sequence * unit_pulse_train

import plotly.graph_objects as go

# Compute the FFT of the modulated signal
# Use rfft for real input signals to get a one-sided spectrum

N_fft = num_samples # Use the same number of points as the signal

signal_fft = np.fft.rfft(signal_modulated, n=N_fft)

# Calculate the corresponding frequencies
freq = np.fft.rfftfreq(N_fft, d=1/sampling_rate)

# Compute the magnitude spectrum (in dB)
magnitude_spectrum_dB = 20 * np.log10(np.abs(signal_fft) + 1e-10) # Add small epsilon to avoid log(0)

# Plot the magnitude spectrum using Plotly
fig = go.Figure(data=go.Scatter(
    x=freq / 1e6,
    y=magnitude_spectrum_dB,
    mode='lines',
    name='Magnitude Spectrum'
))

fig.update_layout(
    title=f'Magnitude Spectrum of PRN Modulated Pulse Train<br><sup>Chip Rate: {chip_rate/1e6:.3f} MHz, T_chip: {T_chip*1e6:.3f} μs, Sampling Rate: {sampling_rate/1e6:.3f} MHz</sup>',
    xaxis_title='Frequency (MHz)',
    yaxis_title='Magnitude (dB)',
    xaxis_range=[0, sampling_rate / (2 * 1e6)] # Limit x-axis to Nyquist frequency
)

HTML(fig.to_html(include_plotlyjs='cdn', full_html=False))
```

### Demodulation of DSSS signals

- The narrowband signal can be recovered by multiplying the received signal by the same spreading code used for modulation.

![](assets/figures/spread_spectrum_demodulation.svg){fig-align="center"}

### Demodulation of DSSS signals (cont'd)

- Mathematically, the demodulation process can be expressed as:

$$
\tiny
m'(t) = s(t) \cdot c(t) = m(t) \cdot c(t) \cdot c(t) = m(t) \cdot \underbrace{(c(t))^2}_{\text{all values are +1 or -1}} = m(t)
$$

- To recover the samples of the narrowband signal, the receiver integrates the demodulated signal over $T_{int} = \min{(T_b, T_{code})}$ (where $T_b$ is the bit duration and $T_{code}$ is the code duration).

$$
\tiny
m'[n] = \frac{1}{T_{int}}\int_{n\cdot T_{int}}^{(n+1)\cdot T_{int}} m'(t) \cdot dt
$$

- The $min$ operator is used to avoid *bit transitions* in the demodulated signal, which would occur if $T_b < T_{code}$.

### Correlation of DSSS signals

- Spreading code has two key uses in GNSS:
  - protects the narrowband signal (i.e. the navigation message) from interference
  - enables the receiver to determine the time of arrival of the signal

- The time of arrival $\tau$ can be determined using spreading code if:
  - The auto-correlation is high when modulation and demodulation codes are aligned
  - The auto-correlation is low when modulation and demodulation codes are misaligned
  - The correlation between two different spreading codes is low (i.e. they are orthogonal)

### Auto-correlation of DSSS signals

- The auto-correlation of a spreading code $c(t)$ is defined as:

$$
R_c(\tau) = \frac{1}{T_{code}}\int_{0}^{T_{code}} c(t) c(t - \tau) dt
$$
